change: Rescale hypot and norm with powers of two when their direct sum of squares loses range.
Clear the float32/float64 sign bit for abs, including negative zero and NaNs.
Use float32 scaling in GLSL, SPIR-V and Metal hypot instead of translating a float64 bit helper.
validation: Independent C bootstrap; 613 focused numerical, shader, GPU-array and web-game checks passed in 33.19 seconds.
reference_coverage: 134 seeded arrays compared with Python math.hypot in native and Node/WebAssembly, default and release. Includes zeros, subnormals, overflow boundaries, infinities, NaNs, mixed exponents and array lengths through 257. Finite results allow 8 ulps; special classifications and positive zero are checked separately.
gpu_coverage: Executed ordinary, 1e30 and 1e-30 inputs, signed zero, infinities and NaNs with local OpenGL ES and Vulkan software drivers, plus native/web CPU fallback. Metal source cross-compilation only; no Apple execution.

limits: Native ordinary finite inputs; extreme-input correctness is covered by independent-reference tests.
Same source for both compilers; alternating fresh processes. Times exclude setup but include result consumption.
No C performance comparison and no universal library throughput claim.

cost: Four million ordinary hypot calls: 16.55 to 28.22 ms default, 15.07 to 20.55 ms release (about 2.9/1.4 ns additional per call). Norm unchanged within noise. Correctness improvement, not a throughput improvement; splitting the slow helper did not recover the old inlining performance.
limits: No correctly-rounded guarantee. The numerical tolerance applies to the recorded cases, not every possible array.
GPU arithmetic uses float32; subnormal treatment depends on the driver. No GPU performance claim.
The prior norm propagates NaN even with infinity; hypot follows the common infinity-dominates-NaN convention.
No changes to dot-product reassociation or compiler-wide inlining thresholds.
The full gate runs in branch CI after push.
rejected: Scaling by the actual largest magnitude falsely overflowed a two-coordinate result near the largest finite float. Power-of-two scaling fixes that case without rounding normal scaled coordinates.
